item.title: Building and Publishing Packages to Posit Package Manager
item.dc:creator: Lisa
item.description:
I wanted to walk through an overview of hosting internally developed packages in your Package Manager. I wanted to lay out the setup options so you can decide which fits your workflow best. I’ll highly recommend the PPM Admin training course, here are its materials that I highly recommend as a companion overview: https://sol-eng.github.io/admin-training-async/ppm_install_03.html

Create the internal packages repos (one for R, one for Python)

Package Manager needs a repo per language. How that repo gets populated is where the options below differ. A single internally developed packages repo can support multiple “sources” meaning that both packages from git (git source) and packages published directly by publishers (internal source) can share a repository.

My recommendation, if you don’t have a strong preference between the options, would be to support both options 1 and 2 by subscribing both sources to the same internal packages repository. Option 1 suits ad hoc or CI-driven publishing where developers want control over timing; Option 2 suits packages that should always reflect the latest version controlled release.

PPM admin steps (one-time setup, per language to host internally developed packages):

rspm create source --name=internal-r-src --type=local
rspm create repo --name=internal-r
rspm subscribe --repo=internal-r --source=internal-r-src

rspm create source --name=internal-py-src --type=local
rspm create repo --name=internal-python
rspm subscribe --repo=internal-python --source=internal-py-src

Option 1: Remote publishing via API key

Developers (or a CI pipeline) push built packages directly to Package Manager whenever they’re ready to publish.

PPM admin steps:

Generate a scoped, expiring token for each publisher or CI system:

rspm create token --description="R package publisher" \
--sources=internal-r-src --expires=90d \
--scope=sources:write --user="<publisher-username>"

Docs: https://docs.posit.co/rspm/admin/authentication/token-authentication.html

Publisher steps:

R packages:

export PACKAGEMANAGER_TOKEN=<token>
export PACKAGEMANAGER_ADDRESS=https://<your-ppm-host>
curl -fLOJH "Authorization: Bearer ${PACKAGEMANAGER_TOKEN}" "${PACKAGEMANAGER_ADDRESS}/__api__/download" && chmod +x rspm
./rspm add --source=internal-r-src --path=/path/to/package_1.0.tar.gz

Python packages:

export TWINE_REPOSITORY_URL=https://<your-ppm-host>/upload/pypi/internal-python-src
export TWINE_USERNAME=__token__
export TWINE_PASSWORD=<token>
twine upload dist/*

Publishing a new version is just re-running the same command with the new build. Package Manager automatically archives the old version and promotes the new one as default.

Docs: https://docs.posit.co/rspm/admin/remote-publishing.html

Option 2: Publishing via version control / git backed

Package Manager subscribes to a version controlled repository and builds the package with no separate publish step for developers.

PPM admin steps:

rspm create source --name=git --type=git
rspm subscribe --repo=internal-r --source=git
rspm create git-builder --source=git --url=git@github.com:org/repo.git --credential=my-key

rspm create source --name=git-py --type=git-python
rspm subscribe --repo=internal-py --source=git-py
rspm create git-builder --source=git-py --url=git@github.com:org/repo.git --credential=my-key

Note: this requires R and/or Python actually installed on the Package Manager server itself, since Package Manager does the build (configured via RVersion/PythonVersion in rstudio-pm.gcfg).

Publisher steps: No additional steps beyond sending the url for the git builder to PPM admin. New versions are picked up automatically.

Docs: https://docs.posit.co/rspm/admin/building-packages.html

Option 3: Developer hands the tarball to the PPM admin, who publishes it manually

This uses the same underlying command as Option 1 (rspm add), but the PPM admin runs it using their own credentials instead of a token scoped to the developer. It’s worth knowing as a fallback, but I don’t recommend it because it makes the PPM admin a bottleneck for every release and lacks a per-publisher audit trail (everything appears to come from the admin account).

Once the internal repo(s) exist: wiring up Workbench and Connect

Creating the repo in Package Manager only makes packages available for install, Workbench and Connect each need to be told the new repo exists before their users/content can actually see it.

Workbench R Packages:

Add the internal repo to /etc/rstudio/repos.conf alongside CRAN:

CRAN=https://<ppm-host>/<cran-repo-name>/latest
Internal=https://<ppm-host>/<internal-r-repo-name>/latest

One thing to check: if Workbench currently sets an R repo via r-cran-repos in rsession.conf instead of repos.conf, that older setting needs to be removed first.

Docs: https://docs.posit.co/rspm/admin/workbench.html#internal-packages-and-cran-packages

Workbench Python packages:

pip: edit /etc/pip.conf, using index-url for the primary index and extra-index-url to add another

[global]
index-url = https://<ppm-host>/<internal-python-repo-name>/latest/simple
extra-index-url = https://<ppm-host>/<pypi-repo-name>/latest/simple

uv: edit /etc/uv/uv.toml, adding an [[index]] block per repo (mark one default = true)

[[index]]  
url = "[https://packagemanager.posit.co/pypi/latest/simple](https://packagemanager.posit.co/pypi/latest/simple)"  
default = true

[[index]]  
url = "https://<ppm-host>/<internal-python-repo-name>/latest/simple"

Docs: https://docs.posit.co/rspm/admin/workbench.html#python-repositories

Connect R and Python packages:

Add a second [RPackageRepository] section in /etc/rstudio-connect/rstudio-connect.gcfg, alongside the existing CRAN one, and then same for Python:

[RPackageRepository "CRAN"]
URL = "https://<ppm-host>/<cran-repo-name>/latest"

[RPackageRepository "internal"]
URL = "https://<ppm-host>/<internal-r-repo-name>/latest"

[PythonPackageRepository "PyPI"]
URL = https://<ppm-host>/<pypi-repo-name>/latest/simple

[PythonPackageRepository "internal"]
URL = https://<ppm-host>/<internal-python-repo-name>/latest/simple

Docs: https://docs.posit.co/connect/admin/r/package-management/index.html#configuring-on-posit-connect and https://docs.posit.co/connect/admin/python/package-management/index.html#python-package-repositories

Hopefully these details are a helpful resource as you navigate publishing internally developed packages to your package manager instance.

item.title: Sharepoint Access article 20
item.dc:creator: Lisa
item.description:
Note

Disclaimer: This page discusses Microsoft-developed open source packages. For R, the Microsoft365R package was at version 2.4.1 and AzureAuth at version 1.3.4 at the time of initial writing. For Python, the Office365-REST-Python-Client library is the Microsoft-recommended approach. Readers should refer to the Microsoft365R package documentation and Office365-REST-Python-Client documentation for the most up-to-date information.

Introduction

Microsoft 365 is a subscription extension of the Microsoft Office product line with cloud hosting support.

  • For R users, the Microsoft-supported method is the Microsoft365R package developed by Hong Ooi. It supports access to Teams, SharePoint Online, Outlook, and OneDrive.
  • For Python users, the recommended approach is the Office365-REST-Python-Client library, which provides access to Microsoft 365 services including SharePoint Online.

This article describes approaches for authentication to Microsoft 365 for use with the Posit professional products. Examples for both R and Python are included, along with guidance on using managed credentials in Posit Workbench and Posit Connect for secure, enterprise-friendly access patterns.

Summary

  • Authentication for Microsoft365R is through Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform through registered applications. This grants developers access to the underlying Microsoft API for programmatic access to Microsoft resources.
  • The registered application will be used to authenticate in to the Microsoft Azure cloud platform using any of the four main authentication approaches that are supported by Microsoft365R. You will select the approach that fits the types of content being built and your organizations security requirements and add the needed permissions, redirect URLs, etc in order to enable access.
  • The steps for registering a custom app are provided in this Microsoft page.
  • Graph permissions will need to be granted as specified in the app registrations page. Depending on your organization’s security policy, access will likely need to be granted by your Microsoft Azure Global Administrator. Depending on the authentication method selected, these could be user/delegated level permissions, or Graph application level permissions.
  • Consult our page on securing credentials to review best practices for guarding the authentication details.

Authentication Options

Note

Discussion between the developers and the Global Azure Administration team about your organization’s content and security requirements is important to decide which approach will work best for your needs.

There are several authentication approaches available. For Posit users, managed credentials through Posit Workbench or Posit Connect are the recommended primary option for enterprise deployments.

Authentication options using active authentication (good for interactive content and sessions)

Method auth_type (R / Python) Permissions Microsoft Setup Needed Capability
Managed Credentials: Workbench (Delegated) rstudioapi::getDelegatedAzureToken() / client.oauth.get_delegated_azure_token() Delegated (User) Azure app registration (admin configures), user signs in once via SSO Interactive Workbench sessions and jobs launched from them
Managed Credentials: Connect (Viewer OAuth) connectapi::get_oauth_credentials() / client.oauth.get_credentials() Delegated (Viewer) Azure app registration (admin configures an OAuth integration) Published Connect content; each viewer’s own SharePoint permissions apply
User Sign-in Flow: Default default / with_interactive() Delegated (User) Redirect URLs, user permissions Interactive only (local IDE, Workbench, interactive Shiny/Streamlit)
User Sign-in Flow: Device Code device_code / with_device_flow() Delegated (User) Enable mobile and desktop flows, user permissions Interactive only (local IDE, Workbench)

Authentication options using embedded credentials (good for static content)

Method auth_type (R / Python) Permissions Microsoft Setup Needed Capability
Managed Credentials: Connect (Service Account OAuth) Same as above, configured for a shared service identity Delegated (Service Account) Azure app registration + service account configured in the integration Scheduled reports and content where a shared, non-viewer-specific identity is appropriate
Service Principal / Client Secret client_credentials / with_client_secret() Application Application permissions, client secret Scheduled/non-interactive, APIs, background jobs
Service Account / Embedded Credentials resource_owner / with_username_and_password() Delegated (Service Account) Service account credentials in code Scheduled/non-interactive content

Authentication Background

Authentication for Microsoft365R is through Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform through a registered application. This grants developers access to the underlying Microsoft API for programmatic access to Microsoft resources.

Within this page “application,” also referred to as “app,” refers to a specific part of the Microsoft Authentication Flow. The application is used to:

  1. Obtain an ‘OAuth 2.0’ token by authenticating the requesting user or system
  2. Provide token to access protected APIs for interacting with Microsoft resources

Microsoft365R will use a pre-existing app, “d44a05d5-c6a5-4bbb-82d2-443123722380”, by default that is pre-configured for use with the RStudio IDE and interactive use. Depending on your organizations security it may be blocked and need the Azure Global Administrator to grant access. This default application does not support scheduled reports or development / deployment outside of the RStudio IDE without additional configuration.

A custom app will need to be registered if the default app is blocked or the content being developed is being run outside of the RStudio IDE and/or in a non-interactive context. Depending on the organization’s security policy the custom app registration can be done either by the developer or the Azure Global Administrator. The steps for registering a custom app are provided in this Microsoft page with additional details below.

Under the hood, Microsoft365R is using the AzureAuth and AzureGraph packages, also developed by Hong Ooi, for authentication, token management, and access to the Graph API. In some cases, for example with troubleshooting or to remove interactive prompts in scheduled content, calling those packages directly to manage tokens is useful.

Authentication Configurations

Overview and Setup Resources

Depending on your organization’s security policy, app registration and credential setup may be handled by the developer, may require Azure Global Administrator support, or may need to be entirely managed by your Azure administrator.

Key Resources for Setup:

  • Posit Workbench Managed Credentials (Azure):

    • Admin Setup Guide - Delegated Azure Credentials
    • User Guide - Azure Managed Credentials

  • Posit Connect OAuth Integrations (Microsoft/Azure):

    • Admin Setup Guide - OAuth Integrations
    • User Guide - Managing Integrations

  • Microsoft’s App Registration Guide: Quick Start - Register an Application

  • Microsoft365R Package Guide: Authentication Vignette - comprehensive overview of all authentication approaches

  • App Registration & Permissions: Microsoft365R App Registration Reference - highly recommended detailed breakdown of required permissions, redirect URIs, platform configurations, and best practices for each authentication method

The app registration reference provides crucial details on: - Exact Graph API permissions needed for different use cases - Proper redirect URI configuration for different deployment scenarios - Platform-specific setup (Desktop, Web, Mobile) - Scope and consent configuration - Token requirements and refresh strategies

Managed Credentials (Recommended for Enterprise)

For Posit Workbench Admins: Set up managed credentials to provide users with seamless Azure authentication. Azure credentials are automatically available from Workbench sessions when it has been configured with the appropriate permissions. Tokens are accessible on demand using the Software Development Kit (SDK) functions available to users.

  • Workbench Admin Setup - Delegated Azure Credentials

For Posit Connect Admins: Configure OAuth integrations to enable viewer-based authentication for published content. Each viewer authenticates with their own identity for data access.

  • Connect Admin Setup - OAuth Integrations

Individual Authentication Methods

The following sections describe setup and usage for each direct authentication approach. These are typically used when managed credentials are not available. For first-time setup, reference the app registration guide linked above.

User Sign-in Flow: Default

A custom app can be created or the default app registration “d44a05d5-c6a5-4bbb-82d2-443123722380” that comes with the Microsoft365R package can be used. The user permissions will need to be enabled as detailed in the app registrations page. Depending on your organization’s security policy, access to your tenant may need to be granted by an Azure Global Administrator. Additionally, Redirect URLs will need to be added through Azure under App Registrations -> select your app -> Authentication -> Platform configurations -> Mobile and desktop applications ->Add URI as well as also enabling nativeclient.

For adding Redirect URLs, which will give a typical web-app authentication experience for interactive applications:

  • For RStudio Desktop the URL is: http://localhost:1410/.
  • For Connect and Workbench, as well as any non-local connections, the URL will be of the form https://myserver.com/myapplication. An SSL certificate will be required by Azure. A wildcard could be used where appropriate for server-wide access.
  • For content hosted in shinyapps.io this would be of the form https://youraccount.shinyapps.io/appname (including the port number if specified).

User Sign-in Flow: Device Code

A custom app can be created. User permissions will need to be enabled as detailed in the app registrations page. Depending on your organization’s security policy, access to your tenant may need to be granted by an Azure Global Administrator.

Enabling the device code workflow is through the App Registration dashboard in Azure -> click on the created app -> Authentication -> Allow public client flows and setting Enable the following mobile and desktop flows to yes. The device code workflow does not need Redirect URLs. Instead, this method provides a code and a link for the developer to access in a separate browser window (or even on a separate device) for sign-in.

Service Principal / Client Secret

A custom app will need to be registered in Azure with Application permissions. The permissions can be based off of the user permissions but can be assigned as needed for the application and to comply with any security restrictions.

Application permissions are more powerful than user permissions so it is important to emphasize that exposing the client secret directly should be avoided. As a control, using environment variables for storing the client secret is recommended. Connect allows Environment Variables. The variables are encrypted on-disk, and in-memory.

Adding environment variables can be done at the project level with securing deployment through the Connect UI.

Embedded Credentials

A custom app will need to be registered in Azure with User permissions as specified in the app registrations page. Depending on your organization’s security policy, access to your tenant may need to be granted by an Azure Global Administrator.

The credentials being embedded can be a user or a service account, as long as access to the desired content inside Microsoft 365 has been granted. Creating service accounts per content is recommended to enable faster troubleshooting and easier collaboration. As a control, the Username / Password should never be exposed directly in the code, instead using Environment Variables. The variables are encrypted on-disk, and in-memory.

Adding environment variables can be done at the project level with securing deployment through the Connect UI.

Authentication Examples

Managed Credentials (Workbench & Connect Users)

When your administrator has configured managed credentials, you can access Azure services seamlessly without managing tokens or secrets yourself. Credentials are automatically available in your environment and refreshed as needed.

Workbench Users: Access managed credentials by selecting them when launching a session. See User Guide - Azure Managed Credentials for detailed instructions.

Connect Users (SharePoint Examples): Your application automatically has access to OAuth-authenticated resources. See User Guide - Managing Integrations for details.

For practical examples of accessing SharePoint with managed credentials: - SharePoint Integration Cookbook (Python) - SharePoint Integration Cookbook (R)

Accessing the token would be done with:

  • R
  • Python
library(rstudioapi)
library(AzureAuth) 
library(Microsoft365R)
library(AzureGraph)
library(connectapi)

site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"

# check if running on Posit Connect or Workbench
if (Sys.getenv("POSIT_PRODUCT") == "CONNECT") {
    # initialize Connect API client
    client <- connect()
    # read the user-session-token header
    user_session_token <- session$request$HTTP_POSIT_CONNECT_USER_SESSION_TOKEN
    # grab the OAuth Integration access token using the session token
    credentials <- get_oauth_credentials(client, user_session_token)
    token <- credentials$access_token
  } else if (Sys.getenv("POSIT_PRODUCT") == "WORKBENCH") {
    # resource must be Microsoft Graph, since Microsoft365R talks to Graph, not the SharePoint REST API
    credentials <- rstudioapi::getDelegatedAzureToken("https://graph.microsoft.com")
    token <- credentials$access_token
  } else {
    # grab the access token from the SHAREPOINT_TOKEN env var if running locally
    token <- Sys.getenv("SHAREPOINT_TOKEN")
  }

# Create auth token cache directory
create_AzureR_dir()

# wrap the raw access token in a proper AzureAuth token object
sharepoint_token <- get_manual_token(token)

# use the exported token directly, skipping any interactive app/tenant login
site <- get_sharepoint_site(site_url = site_url, token = sharepoint_token)
cat("Connected to:", site$properties$webUrl, "\n")

# List document libraries
site$list_drives()

# Access a document library and list files
drive <- site$get_drive("Documents")
drive$list_items()

# Download a file
drive$download_file("reports/quarterly.xlsx", dest = "quarterly.xlsx")

View getDelegatedAzureToken() documentation.

Note

Watch the package names when installing python packages. pip install posit and pip install office365 will silently install unrelated packages from PyPI that happen to share these names, not the ones used in this article. Always install the exact names for the packages, in this case posit-sdk and Office365-REST-Python-Client to avoid a confusing ModuleNotFoundError after what looks like a successful install.

import os
# pip install posit-sdk 
from posit import connect
from posit.workbench import Client
# pip install Office365-REST-Python-Client 
from office365.sharepoint.client_context import ClientContext

SITE_URL = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
SITE_URL_ROOT = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com" # tenant root, not /sites/YourSite

# check if running on Posit Connect or Workbench
if os.getenv("POSIT_PRODUCT") == "CONNECT":
    client = connect.Client()

    # grab the user session token from headers
    # for streamlit
    user_session_token = st.context.headers.get("Posit-Connect-User-Session-Token")
    # for flask
    # user_session_token = get_request_header("Posit-Connect-User-Session-Token")

    try:
        # fetch the access token using the session token
        access_token = client.oauth.get_credentials(user_session_token).get(
            "access_token"
        )
    # if the refresh token has expired prompt the user to login again
    except connect.errors.ClientError as e:
        if e.error_code == 219:
            print(
                "Your SharePoint refresh token has expired. Please log out and then log back into the integration."
            )
        else:
            print(f"Failed to retrieve SharePoint OAuth credentials: {e}")
        sys.exit(1)
elif os.getenv("POSIT_PRODUCT") == "WORKBENCH":
    client = Client()
    # Resource must match the SharePoint tenant, not Graph, for office365-rest-python-client
    full_token = client.oauth.get_delegated_azure_token(SITE_URL_ROOT)
    # For other resources you would use graph or a different url 
    # full_token = client.oauth.get_delegated_azure_token("https://graph.microsoft.com")
    access_token = full_token["access_token"]
else:
    # grab access token from env var if running locally
    access_token = os.getenv("SHAREPOINT_TOKEN")

# use the acquired access token to authenticate against SharePoint directly,
# skipping any interactive/browser login since we already have a token
def acquire_token():
    return {"access_token": access_token, "token_type": "Bearer"}

ctx = ClientContext(SITE_URL).with_access_token(acquire_token)
web = ctx.web.get().execute_query()
print(f"Connected to: {web.url}")

View get_delegated_azure_token() documentation.

User Sign-in Flow: Default

The user sign-in flow option provides the typical web browser authentication experience. A user will need to be available to interact with the authentication pop-up, making this suitable for interactive applications (such as the local RStudio IDE, Workbench, or an interactive Shiny/Streamlit app), but not for scheduled content.

Warning

Pass tenant explicitly for any custom (non-default) app registration. If omitted, Microsoft365R falls back to the generic /common/ endpoint, which fails with AADSTS50194 for single-tenant apps — the default configuration for a custom app registration, and the setup most readers of this article will actually have.

  • R
  • Python
library(Microsoft365R)

site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
app = "your-app-id"
tenant = "your-tenant-id"

site <- get_sharepoint_site(site_url = site_url, app = app, tenant = tenant)
cat("Connected to:", site$properties$webUrl, "\n")

See the auth vignette for more details.

from office365.sharepoint.client_context import ClientContext

site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
tenant = "your-tenant-id"
client_id = "your-app-id"

ctx = ClientContext(site_url).with_interactive(tenant, client_id)
web = ctx.web.get().execute_query()
print(f"Connected to: {web.url}")

User Sign-in Flow: Device Code

In some interactive cases it may be easier to use the device code flow where the user is prompted with a code and a link which is opened in a separate screen for logging in. For example, for using a Workbench instance deployed without an SSL certificate. This requires interaction from the user and is not applicable for scheduled content. See the auth vignette for more details.

  • R
  • Python
library(Microsoft365R)

site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
app = "your-app-id"
tenant = "your-tenant-id"

site <- get_sharepoint_site(site_url = site_url, app = app, tenant = tenant, auth_type = "device_code")
cat("Connected to:", site$properties$webUrl, "\n")
from office365.sharepoint.client_context import ClientContext

site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
tenant = "your-tenant-id"
client_id = "your-app-id"

# Prints the verification URL and code to the console automatically
ctx = ClientContext(site_url).with_device_flow(tenant, client_id)
web = ctx.web.get().execute_query()
print(f"Connected to: {web.url}")

Service Principal / Client Secret

Content in a non-interactive context (such as scheduled reports) won’t have a user account available for interactive authentication. The Service Principal via Client Secret is the Microsoft-recommended approach for non-interactive scenarios. See the vignette for more details.

Important Security Notes: - Application permissions are more powerful than user permissions, so avoid exposing the client secret directly in code - Store the client secret as an Environment Variable via the Connect UI - For R, use AzureAuth to remove console prompts: AzureAuth::create_AzureR_dir()

  • R
  • Python
library(AzureAuth)
library(AzureGraph)
library(Microsoft365R)

tenant = "your-tenant-id"
site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
app = "your-app-id"

# Add sensitive variables as environmental variables so they aren't exposed
client_secret <- Sys.getenv("MY_CLIENT_SECRET")

# Create auth token cache directory
create_AzureR_dir()

# Create a Microsoft Graph login
gr <- create_graph_login(tenant, app, password = client_secret, auth_type = "client_credentials")

# An example of using the Graph login to connect to a SharePoint site
site <- gr$get_sharepoint_site(site_url)
cat("Connected to:", site$properties$webUrl, "\n")
import os
from office365.sharepoint.client_context import ClientContext

tenant_id = os.getenv("TENANT_ID")
client_id = os.getenv("CLIENT_ID")
client_secret = os.getenv("EXAMPLE_CLIENT_SECRET")
site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"

ctx = ClientContext(site_url).with_client_secret(tenant_id, client_id, client_secret)
web = ctx.web.get().execute_query()
print(f"Connected to: {web.url}")

Embedded Credentials

Content in a non-interactive context (such as scheduled reports) won’t have a user account available for interactive authentication. In cases where Application-level permissions aren’t appropriate for your organization’s security requirements, use embedded credentials instead. See the vignette for more details.

Important Security Notes:

  • Embedded credentials can be a user account or service account; working with your Azure administrator to create service accounts per content is recommended
  • Store credentials as Environment Variables via the Connect UI
  • For R, use AzureAuth to remove console prompts
  • See our best practices guide for environment variable patterns
  • R
  • Python
library(AzureAuth)
library(AzureGraph)
library(Microsoft365R)

tenant = "your-tenant-id"
site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
app = "your-app-id"

# Add sensitive variables as environmental variables so they aren't exposed
user <- Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_MS365R_SERVICE_USER")
pwd <- Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_MS365R_SERVICE_PASSWORD")
app_secret <- Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_MS365R_APP_SECRET")

# Create auth token cache directory, otherwise it will prompt the user on the console for input
create_AzureR_dir()

# Create a Microsoft Graph login
gr <- create_graph_login(tenant, app,
                    username = user,
                    password = pwd,
                    token_args = list(client_secret = app_secret),
                    auth_type = "resource_owner")

# An example of using the Graph login to connect to a SharePoint site
site <- gr$get_sharepoint_site(site_url)
cat("Connected to:", site$properties$webUrl, "\n")
import os
from office365.sharepoint.client_context import ClientContext

tenant_id = os.getenv("TENANT_ID")
client_id = os.getenv("CLIENT_ID")
site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"

# Service account credentials
service_user = os.getenv("EXAMPLE_MS365_SERVICE_USER")
service_password = os.getenv("EXAMPLE_MS365_SERVICE_PASSWORD")

ctx = ClientContext(site_url).with_username_and_password(
    tenant_id, client_id, service_user, service_password
)
web = ctx.web.get().execute_query()
print(f"Connected as service account to: {web.url}")

Troubleshooting Authentication Failures

  • R
  • Python

In the case of authentication failures, clear cached authentication tokens/files:

library(AzureAuth)
library(AzureGraph)

tenant = "your-tenant-id"

AzureAuth::clean_token_directory()
AzureGraph::delete_graph_login(tenant = tenant)

Office365-REST-Python-Client uses MSAL internally for the with_interactive/with_device_flow/with_username_and_password/with_client_secret methods shown above. None of these examples configure a persistent MSAL token cache, so each new ClientContext re-authenticates from scratch (there’s typically nothing on disk to clear unless your own code explicitly set one up).

More SharePoint Examples

Managed Credentials — Recommended

For the best experience in production, use Posit Connect OAuth integrations (viewer-based). Each viewer uses their own SharePoint permissions:

  • Connect and SharePoint Integration Cookbook (Python)
  • Connect and SharePoint Integration Cookbook (R)
  • Workbench and Sharepoint Example Workflows R and Python

Direct Authentication Via Client Secret Static Examples

The authentication method used in these examples can be any of the methods shown above. The documentation on Microsoft365R (for R) and Office365-REST-Python-Client (for Python) contains extensive examples.

  • R
  • Python
library(Microsoft365R)
library(AzureGraph)
library(AzureAuth)

site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
tenant = "your-tenant-id"
app = "your-app-id"
drive_name = "Documents"
file_src = "myfile.csv"

# Add sensitive variables as environment variables so they aren't exposed
client_secret <- Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_SHINY_CLIENT_SECRET")

# Create auth token cache directory
create_AzureR_dir()

# Create a Microsoft Graph login
gr <- create_graph_login(tenant, app, password = client_secret, auth_type = "client_credentials")

# Connect to a SharePoint site
site <- gr$get_sharepoint_site(site_url)

# Get a specific drive (document library)
drv <- site$get_drive(drive_name)

# Download a specific file
drv$download_file(src = file_src, dest = "tmp.csv", overwrite = TRUE)

# List items in the drive
drv$list_items()
drv$list_files()
drv$list_shared_files()
drv$list_shared_items()

# Upload file to SharePoint
drv$upload_file(src = "local_file.csv", dest = "remote_file.csv")
import os
from office365.sharepoint.client_context import ClientContext

site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite"
tenant_id = os.getenv("TENANT_ID")
client_id = os.getenv("CLIENT_ID")
client_secret = os.getenv("EXAMPLE_CLIENT_SECRET")
list_title = "Documents"  # the document library's name
file_path = "Shared Documents/myfile.csv"  # server-relative path

ctx = ClientContext(site_url).with_client_secret(tenant_id, client_id, client_secret)

# Get the document library's root folder
folder = ctx.web.lists.get_by_title(list_title).root_folder

# List files in the folder
files = folder.files.get().execute_query()
for file in files:
    print(file.name)

# Download a file
with open("tmp.csv", "wb") as local_file:
    ctx.web.get_file_by_server_relative_path(file_path).download(local_file).execute_query()

# Upload a file to the same folder
with open("local_file.csv", "rb") as f:
    folder.files.upload(f).execute_query()

# Delete a file
ctx.web.get_file_by_server_relative_path("Shared Documents/local_file.csv").delete_object().execute_query()

Direct Authentication Via Embedded Service Account Credentials (Resource Owner Flow) Static Examples

For legacy Shiny applications or non-Connect deployments using embedded credentials:

# Example using Resource Owner Flow as described in the 'Service Account' section in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Microsoft365R/vignettes/scripted.html 
# Authentication and requirements from Azure side (app set up) described in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/AzureGraph/vignettes/auth.html 
# Access to Sharepoint and how to use the various functions described under `Creating a custom app registration` in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Microsoft365R/vignettes/od_sp.html and the API permissions listed under https://github.com/Azure/Microsoft365R/blob/master/inst/app_registration.md


library(AzureAuth)
library(AzureGraph)
library(Microsoft365R)
library(shiny)
library(DT)
library(spsComps)

tenant = Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_TENANT", "")
app=Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_APP", "")
site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite" # application with user permissions
drive_name = "Documents"
file_src = "penguins_raw.csv"

# Add sensitive variables as environmental variables so they aren't exposed
user <- Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_MS365R_SERVICE_USER")
pwd <- Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_MS365R_SERVICE_PASSWORD")

# Create auth token cache directory, otherwise it will prompt the user on the console for input
create_AzureR_dir()

foo <- function() {
  message("Starting Microsoft Graph login and data pull")

  # create a Microsoft Graph login
  gr <- create_graph_login(tenant, app, 
                           username = user, 
                           password = pwd,
                           auth_type="resource_owner")


  # SharePoint site
  site <- gr$get_sharepoint_site(site_url)

  # Drive 
  drv <- site$get_drive(drive_name)

  # Downloading the file:
  drv$download_file(src = file_src, dest = "tmp.csv", overwrite = TRUE)

  # Reading file into memory
  data <- read.csv(file="tmp.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names=F)

  return(data)
}


ui = fluidPage(
  actionButton("btn1", "Log into Azure and Show Sharepoint File"),
  DT::dataTableOutput("table1")
)

server = function(input,output, session) {
  #Reactive values for the data, https://mastering-shiny.org/index.html is a great resource for learning Shiny
  rv <- reactiveValues()
  rv$data <- NULL

  #btn1
  observeEvent(input$btn1, {
    showNotification("btn1: Running")
    spsComps::shinyCatch({
      rv$data <- foo()
    },

    blocking_level = "error",
    prefix = "My-project" 
    )
  })

  # Output
  output$table1 <- DT::renderDataTable({
    rv$data
  })
}

# Run the application 
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

#### The AzureR packages save your login sessions so that you don’t need to reauthenticate each time. If you’re experiencing authentication failures, you can try clearing the saved data by running the following code:
#
# AzureAuth::clean_token_directory()
# AzureGraph::delete_graph_login(tenant="mytenant")

Sharepoint and Pins Example

Microsoft resources can be used for hosting data in pins format using pins::board_ms365(). The authentication method used in this example could be swapped out for any of the examples shown above.

library(Microsoft365R)
library(pins)

tenant = Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_TENANT", "")
app=Sys.getenv("EXAMPLE_APP", "")
site_url = "https://yourorg.sharepoint.com/sites/YourSite" # application with user permissions

# Create a Microsoft Graph login
site <- get_sharepoint_site(site_url = site_url, app = app, tenant = tenant, auth_type = "device_code")

# An example getting the default drive 
doclib <- site$get_drive()

# Connect ms365 as a pin board. If this folder doesn't already exist it will be created on execution. 
board <- board_ms365(drive = doclib, "general/project1/board")

# Write a dataset as a pin to SharePoint
board %>% pin_write(mtcars, "mtcars", description = "This is a test")

# View the metadata of the pin we just created 
board %>% pin_meta("mtcars")

# Read the pin
test <- board %>% pin_read("mtcars")

Other Azure service URL’s

To retrieve a token a user needs to specify the URI for the Azure service. Here is a table for common resources (as taken from here):

Azure Service Resource URI
Azure Storage https://storage.azure.com
Azure Key Vault https://vault.azure.net
Azure SQL Database https://database.windows.net
Azure Management https://management.azure.com
Microsoft Graph https://graph.microsoft.com

Other Microsoft 365 Related Resources

There are a few cases not covered in this article where the below resources may be useful:

  • For readers interested in directly interacting with the Graph API, the Microsoft page on Working with SharePoint sites in Microsoft Graph is a useful starting reference.

  • For Python users the Microsoft REST API is the Microsoft-developed and recommended method for accessing Microsoft 365 resources. Note that SharePoint access is using the older SharePoint 2013 REST API.

  • Mapping SharePoint, OneNote, or other systems as a network drive to the hosting server could be considered, using a third-party developed program such as expandrive. Note that this method also relies on application registration and it is unclear to this author how authentication is handled.

item.title: Workbench and Azure managed credentials
item.dc:creator: Lisa
item.description:
Configure Workbench Custom OAuth for Programmatic SharePoint Data Access w/o Changing Auth Providers

Background

For connecting to SharePoint data from Workbench there are two main options:

Option 1: Migrate to Entra ID login + delegated Azure credentials (recommended, fully supported)

This requires Workbench’s login authentication to be Microsoft Entra ID via OpenID Connect, and uses delegated credentials so a user’s own sign-in grants their R/Python sessions access to Azure resources.This is the fully supported feature option.

  • Configure Entra ID with OpenID Connect (Quick Start)
  • Delegated Azure Credentials (Admin Guide)
  • Using Azure Delegated Credentials in Sessions (User Guide)

Option 2: Custom OAuth Integration (possible, but a preview feature)

This would keep allow any existing login setup with an added separate OAuth integration pointed at an Azure app registration purely for data access. However, this feature is currently in preview: it’s not yet fully supported for production use and could see breaking changes in future releases. It’s an option to explore if you need to avoid a login migration, but it comes with that tradeoff.

  • Custom OAuth Credentials (Admin Guide)
  • Custom OAuth Integrations (User Guide)

For a side-by-side comparison of all credential/provider options, this overview page is a good reference:

  • Managed Credentials Overview

Overview

This guide walks you through configuring Posit Workbench to use Option 2: Custom OAuth integration with Azure Entra ID for programmatic access to Microsoft SharePoint and Microsoft Graph APIs. This integration allows users to authenticate normally with passwords or OpenID Connect, while gaining the ability to request OAuth tokens within R and Python sessions for accessing SharePoint data.

Important: This is not single sign-on (SSO) or OAuth-based login. Users authenticate to Workbench using their normal credentials with whichever login method has been chosen. The Custom OAuth integration enables them to obtain specific tokens for programmatic Microsoft Graph access.

What You Will Accomplish

By the end of this guide, your Workbench server will:

  • Authenticate users to Workbench using whichever auth method you currently have set up
  • Authenticate programmatically for data access with Microsoft Entra ID using OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow
  • Store OAuth tokens in the Workbench session database
  • Allow users to retrieve tokens within R and Python sessions via rstudioapi::getOAuthCredentials()
  • Support delegated permissions for SharePoint and Microsoft Graph API access

Prerequisites

Before you begin, ensure you have:

  • Workbench installed and accessible via HTTPS with a valid SSL certificate
  • Administrative access to Azure Entra ID with permission to create and modify applications and grant admin consent
  • Administrative command line access to the Workbench server with sudo privileges
  • Valid SSL certificate with verified HTTPS access for Workbench redirect callback URL
  • Network connectivity between Workbench and Azure Entra ID on port 443 (HTTPS)

SSL Certificate Note: Self-signed certificates are supported for testing, but production environments should use a CA-signed certificate.

Architecture Overview

┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  Workbench Browser          │
│  ├─ HTTPS enabled           │
│  ├─ oauth-clients.conf      │
│  └─ User Sessions (R/Python)│
└──────────────┬──────────────┘
               │ (HTTPS)
               ↓
     ┌─────────────────────────────┐
     │  Azure Entra ID             │
     │  ├─ App Registration        │
     │  ├─ Delegated Permissions   │
     │  ├─ Redirect URI            |
     │  └─ OAuth 2.0 Endpoints     │
     └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                    │ (Token Exchange)
                    ↓
     ┌─────────────────────────────┐
     │  Microsoft Graph API        │
     │  SharePoint Online          │
     └─────────────────────────────┘

Step 1: Create and Configure the Azure Entra ID Application

1.1: Register the Application

  1. Sign in to the Azure portal
  2. Navigate to Azure Entra ID > App registrations
  3. Click + New registration
  4. Enter the following details:
    • Name: e.g., Posit-Workbench-SharePoint-OAuth
    • Supported account types: Select “Accounts in this organizational directory only”
    • Redirect URI: Leave blank for now, you’ll add it in the next step
  5. Click Register

1.2: Configure the Redirect URI

  1. From the app registration Overview page, select + Add a Redirect URI (or go to Authentication)

  2. Click + Add a platform > Web

  3. Enter your Workbench redirect URI:

    https://<workbench-hostname>/oauth_redirect_callback

    Replace <workbench-hostname> with your actual Workbench domain (e.g., workbench.example.com)

  4. Critical: The redirect URI must:

    • Use HTTPS (not HTTP)
    • Include the exact path /oauth_redirect_callback
    • Match exactly what you configure in Workbench (case-sensitive)
    • Be a publicly resolvable domain (localhost is not accepted by Azure in production)
    • In the case of having Workbench behind a proxy should be the proxy URL apprpriately configured to allow traffic to pass

  5. Click Save

1.3: Create a Client Secret

  1. From the app registration, go to Manage > Certificates & secrets
  2. Click + New client secret
  3. Enter a description (e.g., “Workbench OAuth”)
  4. Set Expires: to “24 months” or your organization’s standard
  5. Click Add
  6. Immediately copy the secret value (shown under Value, not Client ID)
    • Important: This secret is only displayed once. Store it securely; you will need it for Workbench configuration.

1.4: Copy Your IDs

From the app registration Overview page, copy and save: - Application (client) ID - Directory (tenant) ID

You will need these for Workbench configuration.

1.5: Configure API Permissions

  1. Go to Manage > API permissions

  2. Click + Add a permission

  3. Select Microsoft Graph from the list

  4. Select Delegated permissions

  5. Search for and select the following permissions:

    • User.Read — Read user profile information
    • Files.Read.All — Read files in SharePoint and OneDrive
    • Sites.Read.All — Read SharePoint sites
    • offline_access — Required for token refresh capability
    • Any others that may be needed to support access as detailed here

  6. Click Add permissions

  7. After adding permissions, click Grant admin consent for [Your Organization]

  8. Click Yes to confirm

Important: Admin consent is required for Custom OAuth to function. User consent alone is insufficient.

Step 2: Prepare the Client Secret

You have two options for handling the client secret in your configuration: encrypt it or use it in plain text.

Option A: Encrypt the Client Secret (Recommended)

On your Workbench server with sudo access, use the built-in encryption utility:

sudo rstudio-server encrypt-password

When prompted, enter the client secret you copied from Azure. The command will output an encrypted value. Copy this encrypted value for use in Step 3 below.

Option B: Use Plain Client Secret (Acceptable for Testing)

You can also use the client secret directly in the configuration file without encryption.

Note: For production environments, encryption is strongly recommended. Choose the option that best fits your security requirements and environment.

For this guide, we’ll show examples using Option A (encrypted), but the steps work the same with a plain secret.

Step 3: Create the Custom OAuth Configuration File

This is the only configuration file required for Custom OAuth. Your existing authentication method (PAM, LDAP, Active Directory, or any other) will continue to work unchanged. The Custom OAuth integration is independent of login authentication.

Create /etc/rstudio/oauth-clients.conf with the following structure:

# ============================================================================
# Workbench Custom OAuth Clients Configuration
# ============================================================================
# This file defines OAuth integrations for programmatic access to external
# services. The section name appears in the UI under Managed Credentials.
# ============================================================================

[sharepoint-oauth]

# Display name in Workbench UI (Settings > Managed Credentials > Custom OAuth)
name=SharePoint OAuth Integration

# Azure Entra ID Application (client) ID from Step 1.4
client-id=<APPLICATION_CLIENT_ID>

# Client secret from Step 1.3 (encrypted or plain)
# For security, it is recommended to encrypt using: sudo rstudio-server encrypt-password
# Then paste the encrypted value here
client-secret=<CLIENT_SECRET_OR_ENCRYPTED_VALUE>

# Azure OAuth 2.0 authorization endpoint (replace TENANT_ID with yours)
authorize-url=https://login.microsoftonline.com/<TENANT_ID>/oauth2/v2.0/authorize

# Azure OAuth 2.0 token endpoint (replace TENANT_ID with yours)
token-url=https://login.microsoftonline.com/<TENANT_ID>/oauth2/v2.0/token

# Scopes for programmatic access (space-separated, explicit URLs)
# CRITICAL: Must be explicit URLs, not .default scope
# Why? Custom OAuth uses delegated permissions. The .default scope only works 
# with application-level permissions. Use individual, explicit scope URLs.
scopes=https://graph.microsoft.com/User.Read https://graph.microsoft.com/Files.Read.All https://graph.microsoft.com/Sites.Read.All offline_access

# Token endpoint authentication method
# Use client-secret-basic (most reliable)
token-endpoint-auth-method=client-secret-basic

Replace: - <APPLICATION_CLIENT_ID> with your Application (client) ID from Step 1.4 - <CLIENT_SECRET_OR_ENCRYPTED_VALUE> with either: - The encrypted value from Step 2.1 (recommended), OR - The plain client secret from Step 1.3 (less secure, not recommended for production) - <TENANT_ID> with your Directory (tenant) ID from Step 1.4 (appears twice in URLs)

Step 4: Configure SSL/TLS and Launcher Sessions

Custom OAuth requires HTTPS for the OAuth redirect callback. Additionally, you need to configure launcher sessions for Custom OAuth to function properly with session management.

4.A: SSL/TLS Configuration

Ensure your Workbench has SSL configured in rserver.conf. If you already have HTTPS set up, verify these settings are present:

# ============================================================================
# SSL/TLS Configuration (REQUIRED for OAuth redirect callback)
# ============================================================================

# Enable SSL
ssl-enabled=1

# Path to SSL certificate
ssl-certificate=/path/to/your/certificate.crt

# Path to SSL certificate key
ssl-certificate-key=/path/to/your/certificate.key

# TLS protocol versions (explicit specification required)
ssl-protocols=TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3

# HTTPS port (standard is 443, or 8443 if running without root)
www-port=443

4.B: Launcher Sessions Configuration

Add the following launcher configuration to /etc/rstudio/rserver.conf. This enables session management which Custom OAuth depends on:

# ============================================================================
# Launcher Configuration (REQUIRED for Custom OAuth sessions)
# ============================================================================

# Enable launcher for job execution and sessions
launcher-address=127.0.0.1
launcher-port=5559
launcher-sessions-enabled=1
launcher-default-cluster=Local

# Session callback address - MUST match your OAuth redirect domain exactly
# This is where Workbench sends users after they authenticate with Azure
# It must be HTTPS and must match the redirect URI in your Azure app
launcher-sessions-callback-address=https://<workbench-hostname>

Replace <workbench-hostname> with your actual Workbench domain (e.g., workbench.example.com).

Critical: The launcher-sessions-callback-address must: - Use HTTPS (not HTTP) - Exactly match the redirect URI you configured in Azure (Step 1.2) - Be the publicly resolvable domain (not localhost in production) - Include the full domain name with no trailing slashes

Step 5: Restart Workbench Services

After making configuration changes, restart Workbench:

sudo systemctl restart rstudio-server
sudo systemctl restart rstudio-launcher

Verify that services restarted successfully:

sudo systemctl status rstudio-server
sudo systemctl status rstudio-launcher

Check logs for errors:

sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/rstudio/rstudio-server/rserver.log
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/rstudio/launcher/rstudio-launcher.log

Both services should show active (running).

Step 6: Verify the Configuration

6.1: Test HTTPS Access

From a browser, navigate to your Workbench instance via HTTPS:

https://<workbench-hostname>

Verify that the login page loads without SSL errors.

6.2: Login to Workbench

  1. Login with your existing Workbench credentials using whatever authentication method you currently have configured (PAM, LDAP, Active Directory, Kerberos, SAML, or any other)
  2. Once logged in, click Settings in the top right corner
  3. Select Managed Credentials

You should see a Custom OAuth section with an entry for “SharePoint OAuth Integration” (or whatever name you configured).

6.3: Test OAuth Flow

  1. In Managed Credentials, click the SharePoint OAuth Integration entry
  2. Click “Signing In…”
  3. You will be redirected to Azure for authentication
  4. Sign in with your Azure/Microsoft 365 credentials
  5. Grant permissions when prompted
  6. You will be redirected back to Workbench

After successful authentication, the credential should appear in Managed Credentials without an error icon (red X).

6.4: Retrieve Token in R

In an R session within Workbench, retrieve the OAuth token:

# Get the OAuth token
integration <- rstudioapi::findOAuthIntegration("sharepoint-oauth")
  token <- rstudioapi::getOAuthCredentials(integration$id)
  str(token)

# Verify token structure
str(token)
# Should show: $access_token, $refresh_token, $expires_in, $token_type, etc.

6.5: Use Token for Microsoft Graph API

library(httr2)

# Build request to Microsoft Graph API with token
response <- request("https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me") %>%
  req_headers(Authorization = paste("Bearer", token$access_token)) %>%
  req_perform()

# View user information
content(response)

Reference this page for some examples of interacting with sharepoint data.

Troubleshooting

Problem: OAuth button shows error (red X)

Possible Causes:

  1. Admin consent not granted in Azure
    • Solution: Return to Azure app > API permissions and click “Grant admin consent for [Organization]”
  2. Redirect URI doesn’t match exactly
    • Solution: Verify in Azure app that redirect URI matches exactly what you configured in rserver.conf
    • Check: HTTPS (not HTTP), exact path /oauth_redirect_callback, no trailing slashes
  3. Client secret expired or incorrect
    • Solution: In Azure, create a new client secret and update Workbench configuration
  4. Scopes misconfigured
    • Solution: Verify scopes in oauth-clients.conf are explicit URLs (not .default)
    • Must include offline_access for token refresh

Problem: “Claim is invalid” error from Azure

Root Cause: Corrupted or missing permissions in Azure app

Solution:

  1. Go to Azure app > API permissions
  2. Remove all permissions
  3. Re-add permissions one at a time:
    • User.Read
    • Files.Read.All
    • Sites.Read.All
    • offline_access
  4. Grant admin consent
  5. Wait 30 seconds for Azure to sync
  6. Restart Workbench: sudo systemctl restart rstudio-server

Problem: Cannot retrieve token in R

Solution:

  1. Verify credential appears in Settings > Managed Credentials without error
  2. Check R session is in the same Workbench server where you authenticated
  3. Verify syntax: rstudioapi::getOAuthCredentials("sharepoint-oauth")
    • Section name from oauth-clients.conf must match exactly
  4. Check Workbench logs: sudo journalctl -u rstudio-server -f

Problem: HTTPS connection errors

Solutions:

  • Verify SSL certificate and key paths in rserver.conf are correct
  • Verify certificate is readable by rstudio-server user
  • Test certificate: openssl s_client -connect localhost:443
  • For self-signed certificates, add to system CA bundle or test with curl -k flag

Problem: Sessions fail or won’t connect

Possible Causes:

  1. Launcher not configured
    • Solution: Verify Step 4.B launcher settings are in rserver.conf
    • Check: launcher-sessions-enabled=1 and launcher-default-cluster=Local are set
  2. Launcher callback address doesn’t match OAuth redirect URI
    • Solution: Verify launcher-sessions-callback-address exactly matches your Azure redirect URI
    • Both must use HTTPS and be identical (case-sensitive)
    • Example: If Azure has https://workbench.example.com/oauth_redirect_callback, then launcher-sessions-callback-address=https://workbench.example.com

Problem: OAuth button appears but doesn’t work

If you see a session connection error after authenticating:

  • Verify launcher-sessions-callback-address is configured (Step 4.B)
  • Verify it matches your Azure redirect URI exactly
  • Restart Workbench: sudo systemctl restart rstudio-server rstudio-launcher

Problem: Workbench won’t start

Check logs:

sudo journalctl -u rstudio-server -n 50

Common issues:

  • Configuration file syntax errors (check for missing = signs, invalid section names)
  • File permission issues on oauth-clients.conf or openid-client-secret
  • Client secret file permissions not set to 0600
  • Missing launcher configuration in rserver.conf
  • SSL certificate/key files not found or incorrect paths
  • launcher-sessions-callback-address not set or incorrect format

Configuration Reference

Required for Custom OAuth

Setting File Value Purpose
ssl-enabled rserver.conf 1 Enable HTTPS (required for OAuth callback)
ssl-protocols rserver.conf TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3 Enforce modern TLS versions
ssl-certificate rserver.conf /path/to/cert.crt SSL certificate file path
ssl-certificate-key rserver.conf /path/to/cert.key SSL certificate key file path
[sharepoint-oauth] oauth-clients.conf Section name Appears in UI as credential name
name oauth-clients.conf Display name User-friendly name in Managed Credentials
client-id oauth-clients.conf Azure Application ID OAuth client identifier
client-secret oauth-clients.conf Secret (encrypted or plain) OAuth client credential
scopes oauth-clients.conf Space-separated URLs API permissions to request
token-endpoint-auth-method oauth-clients.conf client-secret-basic Authentication method (tested reliable)
authorize-url oauth-clients.conf Azure OAuth URL Azure authorization endpoint
token-url oauth-clients.conf Azure OAuth URL Azure token endpoint

How the OAuth Flow Works

User in Workbench
     ↓
Settings > Managed Credentials > Custom OAuth
     ↓
Clicks "SharePoint OAuth Integration" → "Signing In..."
     ↓
Browser redirected to:
  https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant_id}/oauth2/v2.0/authorize?
  client_id={CLIENT_ID}&
  redirect_uri=https://{workbench_hostname}/oauth_redirect_callback&
  scope=https://graph.microsoft.com/User.Read ...&
  response_type=code
     ↓
User logs in to Azure
     ↓
User grants permissions
     ↓
Azure redirects back to:
  https://{workbench_hostname}/oauth_redirect_callback?code={AUTH_CODE}
     ↓
Workbench exchanges AUTH_CODE for token
  POST https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant_id}/oauth2/v2.0/token
  client_id={CLIENT_ID}&
  client_secret={CLIENT_SECRET}&
  code={AUTH_CODE}&
  ...
     ↓
Azure returns:
  { access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, token_type, ... }
     ↓
Token stored in Workbench session database
     ↓
User retrieves in R:
  token ← rstudioapi::getOAuthCredentials("sharepoint-oauth")
     ↓
Use token to access Microsoft Graph / SharePoint:
  Authorization: Bearer {access_token}

Security Considerations

  • Client Secret: Store securely; encrypt using rstudio-server encrypt-password
  • HTTPS Required: All communications must use HTTPS with valid certificates
  • Admin Consent: Admin consent is required; user consent alone will not work
  • Token Storage: Tokens are stored in Workbench session database; follow your organization’s data retention policies
  • Scopes: Request minimum necessary scopes (User.Read, Files.Read.All, Sites.Read.All)
  • Expiration: Tokens expire; use refresh_token for new access tokens

Additional Resources

  • Microsoft Entra ID OAuth 2.0 Documentation
  • Microsoft Graph API Reference
  • Posit Workbench Configuration Reference
  • Posit Custom OAuth Documentation

Summary

You have successfully configured Posit Workbench to use Custom OAuth with Azure Entra ID for programmatic SharePoint data access. Users can now:

  1. Login to Workbench normally
  2. Authenticate via OAuth to Azure to obtain tokens
  3. Use those tokens in R/Python sessions to access Microsoft Graph and SharePoint

The configuration is production-ready. For production deployments, ensure:

  • CA-signed SSL certificate
  • Properly configured firewall rules
  • Regular token rotation and renewal procedures
  • Audit logging for OAuth token usage
  • Backup/recovery procedures

item.title: User access to Workbench
item.dc:creator: Lisa
item.description:
Overview

Posit Workbench gives each user their own Linux session with a home directory, running processes, and file-system permissions. This means every Workbench user must have a corresponding system account on the server (or accessible via network services like System Security Services Daemon (SSSD) or Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)).

Important

Workbench users require local or networked system accounts regardless of what authentication method you use. Enabling user authentication doesn’t also handling user provisioning which needs to be set up separately.

This is different from Posit Connect and Posit Package Manager, which run content under a single service account and do not need per-user system accounts.

How authentication works in Workbench

Workbench uses Linux Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM).

  1. User signs in — either through a direct login form (PAM) or via your SSO provider (SAML, OpenID Connect, or a reverse proxy).
  2. Workbench maps the user to a system account — The authenticated username must match a Linux account on the server.
  3. PAM creates a session — Workbench calls PAM to create a Linux session for the matched system account, which sets up the user’s environment (home directory, groups, and resource limits).

Not all Posit products require local system accounts or PAM. For example, Posit Connect and Shiny Server rely on their own authentication engines and on a single system account for doing their work in most cases, not requiring individualized development environments like the ones offered by Posit Workbench.

Note

When using SSO, OpenID Connect, or proxied authentication, you need to configure PAM sessions to automatically create system accounts on first sign-in. Otherwise, you must provision local system accounts manually before users can sign in.

Pros and cons

Taken from Trevor’s excellent slide deck ~July 2025

Strategy Pros Cons
Manual Linux user accounts Simple, quick to set up Doesn’t scale
Corporate LDAP/AD Leverage existing corporate user & group info Set up outside PWB & difficult for some
Corporate SSO OpenID/SAML with SCIM Leverage existing corporate user info & enterprise IT friendly No group info (yet) & more setup required in IdP
Corporate SSO OpenID/SAML with JIT Leverage existing corporate user info & easy set up (once you know the settings) No group info (yet) & less enterprise IT friendly

Key concepts: Authentication vs. Sessions vs. Provisioning

Workbench has three components for successful user access:

Concept What it is
Authentication Verifying user identity (who is this person?)
PAM Sessions Server-side environment setup (home directory, access controls, user permisions)
User Provisioning Creating system accounts automatically vs. manually

Authentication methods

Method When to use Posit Workbench Configuration
Local accounts / PAM Authentication Users have local accounts that already exist PAM Authentication via pam_unix
LDAP or Active Directory Users have LDAP/AD accounts that already exist PAM Authentication via pam_sss or pam_ldap
Kerberos (not SSO) PAM authenticates with Kerberos. PAM + Kerberos via pam_sss or pam_krb5
OAuth2/OpenID Connect (OIDC) Using cloud IdP (Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, etc.) OAuth2/OIDC
SAML Using enterprise SSO (Okta, Microsoft, others) SAML
Proxied Authentication Authentication handled by reverse proxy (Shibboleth, Kerberos) Proxied Authentication

PAM sessions

Even when PAM is not used for authentication (e.g., with SAML or OIDC instead), PAM sessions are still used for home directory access, access controls, and user permissions. A PAM session is a server-side session started on behalf of a user, similar to what a remote shell would do. PAM Sessions]

The steps described in Configuration for user provisioning describe how to set this up.

User provisioning

You must choose how to create (or verify) system accounts. Here’s a quick comparison:

Method When to use How it works Supports groups? Setup
Manual account creation Small deployments or strict IT control IT administrators create accounts with useradd before users sign in ✅ Yes (via local /etc/group or NSS) Create accounts: sudo useradd -m username
LDAP/Active Directory On-premises directory service already exists SSSD connects to LDAP/AD; PAM creates accounts on first login via pam_mkhomedir ✅ Yes (groups from LDAP/AD) SSSD configuration + pam_mkhomedir
Just-in-Time (JIT) Using OIDC/SAML with simple provisioning Workbench creates accounts automatically on first login based on identity provider claims ❌ No Enable: user-provisioning-register-on-first-login=1
SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) Using Okta or Microsoft Entra ID for full account/group sync IdP sends account and group data to Workbench via SCIM API; groups synced automatically ✅ Yes (groups from IdP) SCIM provisioning

item.title: Workbench, LLM’s, and github copilot
item.dc:creator: Lisa
item.description:
Integrating Workbench and Github Copilot

Steps

As an admin, add the following line to /etc/rstudio/rsession.conf to enable the use of copilot in RStudio:

/etc/rstudio/rsession.conf
copilot-enabled=1

Custom SSL certificates (not sure iif applicable or not) will need copilot-ssl-certificates-file= in /etc/rstudio/rsession.conf .

Additionally in order to support Copilot with Positron as an admin Positron Assistant will need to be enabled. To enable the use of copilot in Positron specify the following in the positron-user-settings.json file:

/etc/rstudio/positron-user-settings.json

/etc/rstudio/positron-user-settings.json
{
  "positron.assistant.enable": true,

There are a couple more parameters to consider adding that might be useful:

/etc/rstudio/positron-user-settings.json
    "positron.assistant.consoleActions.enable": true,
    "positron.assistant.showTokenUsage.enable": true,  
    "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.linux": "bash",  
    "extensions.autoUpdate": false,  
    "extensions.autoCheckUpdates": false,
    "positron.assistant.provider.anthropic.enable": false,
    "positron.assistant.provider.githubCopilot.enable": true

From https://positron.posit.co/assistant-getting-started.html#step-2-configure-language-model-providers :

  • Anthropic is enabled by default. Opt out of the positron.assistant.provider.anthropic.enable setting to disable it.
  • GitHub Copilot is enabled by default. Opt out of the positron.assistant.provider.githubCopilot.enable setting to disable it.

However, if users have already created sessions then updating /etc/rstudio/positron-user-settings.json won’t push changes. In that case we should add these settings as enforced settings so they are forced to propagate. Alternatively it can also be worth adding these as enforced settings so that users cannot change them: https://docs.posit.co/ide/server-pro/admin/positron_sessions/user_settings.html#enforced-settings

/etc/rstudio/etc/rstudio/enforced-settings.json

/etc/rstudio/etc/rstudio/enforced-settings.json
{
   "positron.assistant.enable": true, 
   "positron.assistant.consoleActions.enable": true,
   "positron.assistant.showTokenUsage.enable": true,  
   "positron.assistant.gitIntegration.enable": true,
   "positron.assistant.provider.anthropic.enable": false,
   "positron.assistant.provider.githubCopilot.enable": true
}

And then also add to /etc/rstudio/profiles for all users (or change this to specify specific users or groups):

/etc/rstudio/etc/rstudio/enforced-settings.json

/etc/rstudio/profiles
[*]
positron-enforced-settings = /etc/rstudio/enforced-settings.json

The presence of /etc/rstudio/positron-user-settings.json will automatically create settings for every user upon launching positron so that they only need to select and sign into copilot once. more technically, the positron-user-settings.json is merged with a user’s existing settings.json, and importantly, once a setting has been merged, future template changes won’t propagate to users who already have that setting defined which will require them to update manually.

For RStudio, users will then need to:

  1. Navigate to Tools > Global Options > Copilot
  2. Check “Enable GitHub Copilot”
  3. Wait a moment (or close and repoen the global options menu) for the sign-in field to populate
  4. Click “Sign In” and follow the device authentication flow at https://github.com/login/device

This will give the Rstudio and copilot integration experience with ghost editing: https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/tools/copilot.html#using-copilot

Chattr is a really cool open source R package sponsored byPosit that can help extend the integration into interactive chat sessions: https://mlverse.github.io/chattr/

Reference: https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/tools/copilot.html

For Positron, users will need to:

Follow the getting started steps in the Positron User Guide:

  1. Open positron assistant (the robot logo in the extensions pane)
  2. Configure Language Model Providers
  3. Select GitHub Copilot as the model provider.
  4. Select the Sign in button to initiate GitHub’s OAuth authentication flow.

Users then can open Positron assistant and use it. Unfortunately Databot was developed and tested with Claude models, and is only available for use with that model family. But Positron Assistant should cover the same use cases.

There’s some useful troubleshooting information around authentication to Copilot here: https://docs.posit.co/ide/server-pro/user/positron/guide/positron-assistant.html#github-copilot-authentication-change

It maybe useful to note that users who previously signed into GitHub within Positron (for Copilot or other integrations) must sign out and sign back in after upgrading to version 2026.01.1

Other LLM providers

For other LLM providers the integration is only through Positron and is Positron Assistant (Databot for Claude specifically).

Here an example /etc/rstudio/positron-user-settings.json:

/etc/rstudio/positron-user-settings.json
{
  "positron.assistant.enable": true, 
  "positron.assistant.enabledProviders": ["amazon-bedrock"],
  "positron.assistant.enabledProviders": [
        "amazon-bedrock",
        "openai-api",
    ]
}

There may be additional settings to consider adding:

  {
  "positron.assistant.enable": true, 
  "positron.assistant.models.preference.byProvider": {
    "anthropic-api": "Claude Sonnet 4.5",
    "openai-api": "gpt-4o"
  },
  "positron.assistant.models.include": [
  "claude",
  "GPT-4o",
  "^claude.*opus"
  ],
  "positron.assistant.enabledProviders": ["amazon-bedrock"],
  "positron.assistant.enabledProviders": [
    "azure",
    "mistral",
    "ollama",
    "openai"
  ],
  "positron.assistant.gitIntegration.enable": true,
  "positron.assistant.testModels": true,
  "positron.assistant.followups.enable": false,
  "positron.assistant.consoleActions.enable": true,
  "positron.assistant.showTokenUsage.enable": true,
  "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.linux": "bash",
  "extensions.autoUpdate": false,
  "extensions.autoCheckUpdates": false,
}

User will need to run the command Positron Assistant: Configure Language Model Providers in the Command Palette.

Consider ading these as enforced settings so that users cannot change them: https://docs.posit.co/ide/server-pro/admin/positron_sessions/user_settings.html#enforced-settings

/etc/rstudio/etc/rstudio/enforced-settings.json

/etc/rstudio/etc/rstudio/enforced-settings.json
{
  "files.autoSave": true
}

Disabling Positron Assistant

Add enforced settings to helm values.yaml

  config:
    server:
      rserver.conf:
        admin-enabled: 1

      # Add enforced settings JSON file
      enforced-settings.json: |
        {
          "positron.assistant.enable": false,
             "extensions.allowed": {
                 "posit.assistant": false,
              }
    },

The key here to get positron assistant to not show up being:

        }
  # Reference the enforced settings in profiles
      profiles:
        "*":
          positron-enforced-settings: /mnt/configmap/rstudio/enforced-settings.json
  
"extensions.allowed": {
        "posit.assistant": false,
    },

item.title: Examples for connecting to Snowflake using Managed Credentials
item.dc:creator: Lisa
item.description:
Check that credentials are cached in your session with this command, run in terminal: env | grep SNOWFLAKE

Here is an example from https://docs.posit.co/ide/server-pro/user/posit-workbench/managed-credentials/snowflake.html The Snowflake CLI wraps Snowflake SQL and provides configuration management and data access tools.

# List connections
snow connection list

And then here is an easy one for R:

library(DBI)
library(odbc)

conn <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake())
DBI::dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT CURRENT_USER()")

Here is the Shiny app (save as an app.R file, you’ll also need to change WAREHOUSE, DB, and SCHEMA and add SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT as an environment variable and add the snowflake integration):


library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(DBI)
library(odbc)
library(dplyr)
library(connectcreds)

ui <- page_fluid(
  title = "Snowflake test",
  card(
    card_header("who am i"),
    verbatimTextOutput("whoami")
  ),
  card(
    card_header("connection details"),
    verbatimTextOutput("connection_info")
  ),
  card(
    card_header("data"),
    tableOutput("data")
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
 
  # Define connection parameters
  WAREHOUSE <- "DEFAULT_WH"
  DB <- "LENDING_CLUB"
  SCHEMA <- "PUBLIC"
  ACCOUNT <- Sys.getenv("SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT")
 
  con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::snowflake(),
                        # connection_name = "workbench",
                        warehouse = WAREHOUSE,
                        account = ACCOUNT,
                        database = DB,
                        schema = SCHEMA
  )
 
 
  output$whoami <- renderText ({
    whoami <- (
      DBI::dbGetQuery(con, 'SELECT CURRENT_USER();')
    )
    userrole <- (
      DBI::dbGetQuery(con, 'SELECT CURRENT_ROLE();')
    )
    paste0("Hello, ", whoami, ". Your role is: ",userrole)
  })
 
  output$connection_info <- renderText({
    con_info <- paste(capture.output(print(con)), collapse = "\n")
    paste0(
      "Warehouse: ", WAREHOUSE, "\n",
      "Account: ", ACCOUNT, "\n",
      "Database: ", DB, "\n",
      "Schema: ", SCHEMA, "\n\n",
      "Connection Object:\n", con_info
    )
  })
 
  output$data <- renderTable ({
    DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SHOW TABLES;")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

item.title: Python binaries
item.dc:creator: Lisa
item.description:
There are many options for installing and managing your python versions.

My current favorite way to do this is with uv. You can run commands that will install and manage your python binaries for you:

# Install a psecific version of python 
uv python install 3.12

# Check aailable and installed python versions 
uv python list

uv will use the Python requirements defined in requires-python in the pyproject.toml file like this:

[[tool.uv.index]]
url = "https://packagemanager.posit.co/pypi/latest/simple"
default = true

[project]
name = "python-shiny-app-demo-cicd-github-actions"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12.11"
dependencies = [
    "altair>=5.4.1",
    "anywidget>=0.9.13",
    "pandas>=2.2.3",
    "shiny>=1.2.1",

  • There is documentation on the binaries here: https://gregoryszorc.com/docs/python-build-standalone/main/running.html#obtaining-distributions
